claim: Most age-related human diseases are accompanied by a decline in cellular organelle integrity, including impaired lysosomal proteostasis and defective mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Most age-related human diseases are accompanied by a decline in cellular organelle integrity, including impaired lysosomal proteostasis and defective mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature on aging and organelle dysfunction.

claim: Narrow-sense heritabilities were recently estimated as 56% for T2D, 46% for general hypertension, and 41% for atherosclerosis.
source: for example, narrow-sense heritabilities were recently estimated as 56% for T2D, 46% for general hypertension, and 41% for atherosclerosis (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim cites Wang et al., 2017 as the source of these heritability estimates.

claim: Dysregulation of autophagic proteostasis has been implicated in myriad age-related disorders including neurodegeneration, heart disease, and aging itself.
source: Dysregulation of autophagic proteostasis, for which the lysosome is central, has been implicated in myriad age-related disorders including neurodegeneration, heart disease, and aging itself (Mizushima et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mizushima et al., 2008.

claim: Mouse models deficient for autophagy in the central nervous system show neurodegeneration.
source: mouse models deficient for autophagy in the central nervous system show neurodegeneration (Hara et al., 2006; Komatsu et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hara et al., 2006 and Komatsu et al., 2006.

claim: Endoplasmic reticular (ER) stress has been invoked as central to metabolic syndrome and insulin resistance in T2D.
source: Endoplasmic reticular (ER) stress has been invoked as central to metabolic syndrome and insulin resistance in T2D (Ozcan et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ozcan et al., 2004.

claim: Disruption in the nucleus through increased gene regulatory noise from epigenetic alterations and elevated nuclear envelope 'leakiness' has been implicated in aging.
source: Disruption in the nucleus through increased gene regulatory noise from epigenetic alterations (López-Otín et al., 2013) and elevated nuclear envelope 'leakiness' (D'Angelo et al., 2009) has been implicated in aging.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to López-Otín et al., 2013 and D'Angelo et al., 2009.

claim: Dysfunction in the mitochondria has been invoked as a 'hallmark' of aging.
source: Dysfunction in the mitochondria has even been invoked as a 'hallmark' of aging (López-Otín et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to López-Otín et al., 2013.

claim: Deficits in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) have been documented in aging and age-related diseases as evidenced by in vivo P-NMR measures.
source: In particular, deficits in mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) have been documented in aging and age-related diseases as evidenced by in vivo (Estrada et al., 2012) P-NMR measures (Petersen et al., 2004; Fleischman et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Estrada et al., 2012, Petersen et al., 2004, and Fleischman et al., 2010.

claim: Deficits in mitochondrial OXPHOS have been documented through enzymatic activity in biopsy material.
source: enzymatic activity (Mootha et al., 2003; Schapira et al., 1990; Fannin et al., 1999; Trounce et al., 1989; Kelley et al., 2002; Patti et al., 2003; Stump et al., 2003) in biopsy material
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies measuring enzymatic activity.

claim: Accumulation of somatic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations has been documented in aging and age-related diseases.
source: accumulation of somatic mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations (Bender et al., 2006; Wanagat et al., 2001; Taylor et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bender et al., 2006, Wanagat et al., 2001, and Taylor et al., 2003.

claim: A decline in mtDNA copy number (mtCN) has been documented in aging and age-related diseases.
source: a decline in mtDNA copy number (mtCN) (Ashar et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ashar et al., 2017.

claim: Recessive mutations leading to defects within many cellular organelles can lead to inherited syndromes.
source: Although it has long been known that recessive mutations leading to defects within many cellular organelles can lead to inherited syndromes (e.g. mutations in >300 nuclear DNA (nucDNA)-encoded mitochondrial genes lead to inborn mitochondrial disease; Frazier et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Frazier et al., 2019 and established knowledge.

claim: Mutations in >300 nuclear DNA (nucDNA)-encoded mitochondrial genes lead to inborn mitochondrial disease.
source: mutations in >300 nuclear DNA (nucDNA)-encoded mitochondrial genes lead to inborn mitochondrial disease; Frazier et al., 2019
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Frazier et al., 2019.

claim: Heritability estimates of measures of mitochondrial function are substantial (33–65%).
source: This genetic approach is supported by the observation that heritability estimates of measures of mitochondrial function are substantial (33–65%; Curran et al., 2007; Xing et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Curran et al., 2007 and Xing et al., 2008.

claim: There is no evidence of enrichment for genome-wide association signal in or near mitochondrial genes across any of the analyses performed.
source: To our surprise, we find no evidence of enrichment for genome-wide association signal in or near mitochondrial genes across any of our analyses.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the data analyses performed.

claim: Of 10 tested organelles, only the nucleus shows enrichment among many age-associated traits.
source: Further, of 10 tested organelles, only the nucleus shows enrichment among many age-associated traits
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the data analyses performed.

claim: The enrichment signal from the nucleus emanates primarily from the transcription factors (TFs).
source: with the signal emanating primarily from the transcription factors (TFs).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the data analyses performed.

claim: Genes encoding the mitochondrial proteome tend to be tolerant to heterozygous predicted loss-of-function (pLoF) variation and are 'haplosufficient'.
source: Further analysis shows that genes encoding the mitochondrial proteome tend to be tolerant to heterozygous predicted loss-of-function (pLoF) variation and thus are surprisingly 'haplosufficient' – that is, show little fitness cost with heterozygous pLoF.
evidence: This is a finding of the study based on constraint analysis using gnomAD data.

claim: Nuclear TFs are especially sensitive to gene dosage and are often 'haploinsufficient', showing substantial purifying selection against heterozygous pLoF.
source: In contrast, nuclear TFs are especially sensitive to gene dosage and are often 'haploinsufficient,' showing substantial purifying selection against heterozygous pLoF.
evidence: This is a finding of the study based on constraint analysis using gnomAD data.

claim: Inherited variation influencing gene-regulatory pathways, rather than organelle physiology, plays a role in the inherited risk of common age-associated diseases.
source: Thus, our work highlights inherited variation influencing gene-regulatory pathways, rather than organelle physiology, in the inherited risk of common age-associated diseases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: 24 age-related traits were selected with heritability Z-score > 4.
source: Our final set of prioritized, age-associated traits included 24 genetically diverse, heritable phenotypes (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the trait selection criteria.

claim: Genetic correlations were greater in magnitude than respective phenotypic correlations.
source: In general, genetic correlations were greater in magnitude than respective phenotypic correlations, potentially as GWAS are less sensitive to purely non-genetic factors that may influence phenotypes (e.g. measurement error).
evidence: This is an observation from the correlation analysis with a proposed explanation.

claim: A highly correlated module of primarily cardiometabolic traits was found with high density lipoprotein (HDL) showing anti-correlation.
source: As expected we find a highly correlated module of primarily cardiometabolic traits with high density lipoprotein (HDL) showing anti-correlation (Bulik-Sullivan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis, consistent with prior work.

claim: No traits showed a statistically significant enrichment of mitochondrial genes in the GWAS Catalog analysis.
source: To our surprise, no traits showed a statistically significant enrichment of mitochondrial genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is a finding from the GWAS Catalog enrichment analysis.

claim: Six traits showed a statistically significant depletion of mitochondrial genes in the GWAS Catalog analysis.
source: in fact, six traits showed a statistically significant depletion.
evidence: This is a finding from the GWAS Catalog enrichment analysis.

claim: MitoCarta genes tended to be nominally enriched in fewer traits than the average randomly selected sample of protein-coding genes.
source: Even more strikingly, MitoCarta genes tended to be nominally enriched in fewer traits than the average randomly selected sample of protein-coding genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, empirical p = 0.014).
evidence: This is a finding from the empirical null distribution analysis.

claim: No evidence of enrichment near nucDNA MitoCarta genes was found for any trait tested in UKB using S-LDSC.
source: We found no evidence of enrichment near nucDNA MitoCarta genes for any trait tested in UKB using S-LDSC (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: This is a finding from the S-LDSC enrichment analysis in UKB.

claim: The lack of enrichment among MitoCarta genes was replicated using MAGMA at two different window sizes.
source: We replicated this lack of enrichment using MAGMA at two different window sizes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2E; all q > 0.1).
evidence: This is a finding from the MAGMA enrichment analysis in UKB.

claim: Previously reported enrichment among tissue-specific genes for key traits was successfully replicated using both S-LDSC and MAGMA.
source: We first successfully replicated previously reported enrichment among tissue-specific genes for key traits using both S-LDSC (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and MAGMA (Figure 2—figure supplement 5, Figure 2—figure supplement 6, Appendix 1, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a validation finding showing the methods can detect known enrichments.

claim: Almost all MitoCarta genes have cis-eQTLs in at least one tissue.
source: We finally examined the landscape of cis-expression QTLs (eQTLs) for these genes and found that almost all MitoCarta genes have cis-eQTLs in at least one tissue
evidence: This is a finding from the eQTL analysis using GTEx data.

claim: MitoCarta genes often have cis-eQTLs in more tissues than most protein-coding genes.
source: and often have cis-eQTLs in more tissues than most protein-coding genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 8, Materials and methods, Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the eQTL analysis using GTEx data.

claim: No significant associations on the mtDNA were found for any of the 21 age-related traits available in UKB.
source: We found no significant associations on the mtDNA for any of the 21 age-related traits available in UKB using linear or logistic regression (Materials and methods, Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 9; Source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the mtDNA-GWAS analysis in UKB.

claim: A large number of mtDNA associations were observed for creatinine and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) in UKB.
source: We observed a large number of associations throughout the mtDNA for both traits (p < 1.15 * 10-5, Figure 2—figure supplement 9E).
evidence: This is a finding from the mtDNA-GWAS analysis in UKB, replicating prior results.

claim: The lack of enrichment for MitoCarta genes was successfully replicated across all 10 traits with an available independent cohort GWAS using S-LDSC.
source: We turned to published GWAS meta-analyses (Teslovich et al., 2010; Ehret et al., 2011; Manning et al., 2012; Morris et al., 2012; Schunkert et al., 2011; Estrada et al., 2012; Christophersen et al., 2017; Pattaro et al., 2016; Nalls et al., 2019; Lambert et al., 2013; Supplementary file 1) and successfully replicated the lack of enrichment for MitoCarta genes across all 10 traits with an available independent cohort GWAS using S-LDSC (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is a replication finding from the S-LDSC enrichment analysis in meta-analyses.

claim: No enrichment was observed for MitoCarta genes among well-powered meta-analyses for Parkinson's disease and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Importantly, while we were unable to pursue analyses for PD and Alzheimer's disease in UKB due to limited case counts, we tested MitoCarta genes among well-powered meta-analyses for these disorders (Appendix 1) and observed no enrichment (Figure 2D; all q > 0.1).
evidence: This is a finding from the enrichment analysis in meta-analyses for neurological disorders.

claim: Evidence of heritability enrichment was found in many traits for genes comprising the nuclear proteome.
source: We used S-LDSC to produce heritability estimates for these categories in the UKB age-related disease traits, finding evidence of heritability enrichment in many traits for genes comprising the nuclear proteome (Figure 3A, Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the organelle enrichment analysis.

claim: No other tested organelles besides the nucleus showed evidence of heritability enrichment.
source: No other tested organelles showed evidence of heritability enrichment.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the organelle enrichment analysis.

claim: Variation in or near genes comprising the nuclear proteome explained over 50% of disease heritability on average despite representing only ~35% of tested SNPs.
source: Variation in or near genes comprising the nuclear proteome explained over 50% of disease heritability on average despite representing only ~35% of tested SNPs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Appendix 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the heritability partitioning analysis.

claim: The pattern of heritability enrichment among organelles was successfully replicated using MAGMA in UKB at two window sizes, finding enrichment only among genes related to the nucleus.
source: We successfully replicated this pattern of heritability enrichment among organelles using MAGMA in UKB at two window sizes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2B), again finding enrichment only among genes related to the nucleus.
evidence: This is a replication finding using an alternative method.

claim: Significant heritability enrichment was found within the set of 1804 genes whose protein products are annotated to localize to the chromosome itself.
source: We found significant heritability enrichment within the set of 1804 genes whose protein products are annotated to localize to the chromosome itself (q < 0.1 for nine traits, Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the sub-nuclear compartment enrichment analysis.

claim: Much of the enrichment signal from chromosome-localizing genes is attributable to the subset classified as TFs.
source: Further partitioning revealed that much of this signal is attributable to the subset classified as TFs (Lambert et al., 2018) (1523 genes, q < 0.1 for 10 traits, Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the TF enrichment analysis.

claim: Enrichments among TFs were replicated in several (but not all) corresponding meta-analyses.
source: and also replicated enrichments among TFs in several (but not all) corresponding meta-analyses (Figure 3—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This is a replication finding in independent cohorts.

claim: Non-zinc finger TFs showed enrichment for a highly similar set of traits to those enriched for the whole set of TFs.
source: We generated functional subdivisions of the TFs (Materials and methods, Appendix 1), finding that the non-zinc finger TFs showed enrichment for a highly similar set of traits to those enriched for the whole set of TFs (Figure 3—figure supplement 5D, Figure 3—figure supplement 6B, Figure 3—figure supplement 7B, Figure 3—figure supplement 8B).
evidence: This is a finding from the TF subtype enrichment analysis.

claim: KRAB domain-containing zinc fingers (KRAB ZFs) were largely devoid of enrichment even compared to non-KRAB ZFs.
source: Interestingly, the KRAB domain-containing zinc fingers (KRAB ZFs) (Kapopoulou et al., 2016), which are recently evolved (Figure 3—figure supplement 5H), were largely devoid of enrichment even compared to non-KRAB ZFs (Figure 3—figure supplement 5E, Figure 3—figure supplement 6C, Figure 3—figure supplement 7C, Figure 3—figure supplement 8C).
evidence: This is a finding from the TF subtype enrichment analysis.

claim: Variation within or near non-KRAB domain-containing TF genes has an outsize influence on age-associated disease heritability.
source: Thus, we find that variation within or near non-KRAB domain-containing TF genes has an outsize influence on age-associated disease heritability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TF enrichment analyses.

claim: Significant enrichment for the nucleus was found for parental lifespan (p = 0.0003) using MAGMA.
source: Enrichment analysis of organelles among these traits revealed a significant enrichment for the nucleus for parental lifespan (p = 0.0003) using MAGMA (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the organelle enrichment analysis for aging traits.

claim: A nominally 'suggestive' enrichment for the nucleus was observed for healthspan (p = 0.058) using MAGMA.
source: While we observed only a nominally 'suggestive' enrichment for the nucleus for healthspan (p = 0.058)
evidence: This is a finding from the organelle enrichment analysis for aging traits.

claim: S-LDSC showed significant nuclear heritability enrichment for healthspan (p = 0.0016).
source: S-LDSC showed significant nuclear heritability enrichment (p = 0.0016, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the organelle enrichment analysis for aging traits using an alternative method.

claim: Significant enrichment for TFs and proteins localizing to the chromosome was found in both parental lifespan and healthspan using MAGMA.
source: Analysis of spatial subsets of the nuclear proteome showed significant enrichment for TFs and proteins localizing to the chromosome in both aging phenotypes using MAGMA (Figure 4)
evidence: This is a finding from the sub-nuclear compartment enrichment analysis for aging traits.

claim: The mitochondrion on average is one of the least constrained organelles tested.
source: In agreement with our GWAS enrichment results, we observed that the mitochondrion on average is one of the least constrained organelles we tested, in stark contrast to the nucleus (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a finding from the constraint analysis using gnomAD data.

claim: The nucleus was second only to the set of 'haploinsufficient' genes in the proportion of its genes in the most constrained decile.
source: In fact, the nucleus was second only to the set of 'haploinsufficient' genes (defined based on curated human clinical genetic data; Karczewski et al., 2020, Materials and methods) in the proportion of its genes in the most constrained decile, while the mitochondrion lay on the opposite end of the spectrum (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a finding from the constraint analysis using gnomAD data.

claim: Even the Mendelian mitochondrial disease genes had a high tolerance to pLoF variation on average in comparison to TFs.
source: Interestingly, even the Mendelian mitochondrial disease genes had a high tolerance to pLoF variation on average in comparison to TFs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a finding from the constraint analysis comparing different gene sets.

claim: Highly constrained TF subsets tend to show GWAS enrichment relative to unconstrained subsets for the tested traits.
source: Indeed, explicit inclusion of LOEUF as a covariate in the enrichment analysis model (Materials and methods) reduced the significance of (but did not eliminate) the enrichment seen for the TFs (Figure 5-Figure supplement 2B, Figure 5-Figure supplement 2E, Figure 5-Figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is a finding from the constraint-adjusted enrichment analysis.

claim: The fitness cost of heterozygous variation in mitochondrial genes appears to be far lower than that among TFs.
source: Thus, while disruption in both mitochondrial genes and TFs can produce rare disease, the fitness cost of heterozygous variation in mitochondrial genes appears to be far lower than that among TFs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the constraint analysis findings.

claim: Most of the ~300 inborn mitochondrial disease genes produce disease with recessive inheritance.
source: That MitoCarta genes are 'haplosufficient' and pLoF tolerant (Figure 5A) is consistent with the observation that most of the ~300 inborn mitochondrial disease genes produce disease with recessive inheritance (Frazier et al., 2019) and healthy parents.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Frazier et al., 2019 and is consistent with the study's findings.

claim: The few mitochondrial disorders that show autosomal dominant inheritance are nearly always due to dominant negativity rather than haploinsufficiency.
source: The few mitochondrial disorders that show autosomal dominant inheritance are nearly always due to dominant negativity rather than haploinsufficiency.
evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge of mitochondrial disease genetics.

claim: TFs are known to be haploinsufficient.
source: TFs are known to be haploinsufficient (Seidman and Seidman, 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Seidman and Seidman, 2002.

claim: Regulatory variants modulating TF expression can produce severe Mendelian disease.
source: and even regulatory variants modulating their expression can produce severe Mendelian disease (van der Lee et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to van der Lee et al., 2020.

claim: Enrichment was observed among TFs for 10 different diseases as well as parental lifespan and healthspan.
source: We observe enrichment among TFs for 10 different diseases as well as parental lifespan and healthspan, consistent with observed elevated purifying selection against pLoF variants in these genes.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Variation among TFs may produce disease-associated variants with larger effect sizes than expectation.
source: Our enrichment results combined with pLoF intolerance suggest that variation among TFs may produce disease-associated variants with larger effect sizes than expectation, underscoring their importance as genetic 'levers' for common disease heritability.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Haplosufficiency arises as a consequence of physiology, where system output is inherently buffered against the partial loss of a single gene due to the network organization of metabolic reactions.
source: First, mitochondrial pathways tend to be highly interconnected, and it was already proposed by Wright, 1934 and later by Kacser and Burns, 1981 that haplosufficiency arises as a consequence of physiology, that is, system output is inherently buffered against the partial loss of a single gene due to the network organization of metabolic reactions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wright, 1934 and Kacser and Burns, 1981.

claim: Noncatalytic gene products fall outside the framework of metabolic buffering proposed by Kacser and Burns.
source: Kacser and Burns in fact explicitly mention that noncatalytic gene products fall outside their framework, and we believe that our finding that nucleus-localizing and cytoskeletal genes are the two most pLoF-intolerant compartments is consistent with their assessment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kacser and Burns and is consistent with the study's findings.

claim: Mitochondria may have retained vestigial layers of 'intra-organelle buffering' against genetic variation due to their origin as autonomous microbes.
source: Second, mitochondria were formerly autonomous microbes and hence may have retained vestigial layers of 'intra-organelle buffering' against genetic variation.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: Numerous feedback control mechanisms, including respiratory control, help to ensure organelle robustness across physiological extremes.
source: Numerous feedback control mechanisms, including respiratory control (Chance and Williams, 1955), help to ensure organelle robustness across physiological extremes (Vafai and Mootha, 2012; Balaban et al., 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chance and Williams, 1955, Vafai and Mootha, 2012, and Balaban et al., 1986.

claim: A recent CRISPR screen showed that of the genes for which knock-out modified survival under a mitochondrial poison, there is a striking over-representation of genes that themselves encode mitochondrial proteins.
source: In fact, a recent CRISPR screen showed that of the genes for which knock-out modified survival under a mitochondrial poison, there is a striking over-representation of genes that themselves encode mitochondrial proteins (To et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to To et al., 2019.

claim: Common variation is the largest documented source of narrow-sense heritability, which typically accounts for a majority of disease heritability.
source: Throughout this study, we have tested for enrichment among inherited common variant associations near genes via an additive genetic model. We acknowledge the limitations of focusing on a specific genetic model and variant frequency regime, though note that common variation is the largest documented source of narrow-sense heritability, which typically accounts for a majority of disease heritability (Golan et al., 2014; Polderman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Golan et al., 2014 and Polderman et al., 2015.

claim: A previous rare variant analysis in T2D failed to show enrichment among OXPHOS genes.
source: While rare variants may prove to be instructive, it is notable that a previous rare variant analysis in T2D (Fuchsberger et al., 2016) failed to show enrichment among OXPHOS genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Fuchsberger et al., 2016.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction is documented in brain or heart infarcts following blood vessel occlusion in laboratory-based models.
source: For example, mitochondrial dysfunction is documented in brain or heart infarcts following blood vessel occlusion in laboratory-based models (Solenski et al., 2002; Flameng et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Solenski et al., 2002 and Flameng et al., 1991.

claim: Pharmacological blockade of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore can mitigate reperfusion injury and infarct size.
source: Clearly, mitochondrial genetic variants do not influence infarct risk in this laboratory model, but pharmacological blockade of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore can mitigate reperfusion injury and infarct size (Weinbrenner et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Weinbrenner et al., 1998.

claim: Most human progeroid syndromes result from monogenic defects in nuclear components.
source: Our finding that the nucleus is the only organelle that shows enrichment for common age-associated trait heritability builds on prior work implicating nuclear processes in aging. Most human progeroid syndromes result from monogenic defects in nuclear components (Kubben and Misteli, 2017) (e.g. LMNA in Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome, TERC in dyskeratosis congenita)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kubben and Misteli, 2017.

claim: Telomere length has long been observed as a marker of aging.
source: and telomere length has long been observed as a marker of aging (Garcia et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Garcia et al., 2007.

claim: Heritability enrichment of age-related traits among gene regulators is consistent with the epigenetic dysregulation and elevated transcriptional noise observed in aging.
source: Heritability enrichment of age-related traits among gene regulators is consistent with the epigenetic dysregulation (Han and Brunet, 2012) and elevated transcriptional noise (López-Otín et al., 2013; Bahar et al., 2006) observed in aging (e.g. SIRT6 modulation influences mouse longevity and metabolic syndrome; Kanfi et al., 2012; Kanfi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Han and Brunet, 2012, López-Otín et al., 2013, Bahar et al., 2006, Kanfi et al., 2012, and Kanfi et al., 2010.

claim: A very large fraction of common disease-associated loci corresponds to the non-coding genome.
source: An important role for gene regulation in common age-related disease is in agreement with both the observation that a very large fraction of common disease-associated loci corresponds to the non-coding genome and the enrichment of disease heritability in histone marks and TF binding sites (Finucane et al., 2015; Karczewski et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Finucane et al., 2015 and Karczewski et al., 2013.

claim: Disease heritability is enriched in histone marks and TF binding sites.
source: An important role for gene regulation in common age-related disease is in agreement with both the observation that a very large fraction of common disease-associated loci corresponds to the non-coding genome and the enrichment of disease heritability in histone marks and TF binding sites (Finucane et al., 2015; Karczewski et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Finucane et al., 2015 and Karczewski et al., 2013.
